cues.text:
In sixteen forty-two, two Dutch ships
approached a
mountainous coast in the southern Pacific.
Their commander, Abel Tasman,

had never seen these distant islands
before.
But as the ships sailed along the coast,
smoke rose from the land.
Someone was already living there.
For the Māori, these islands were home.

Their ancestors had crossed the Pacific
from East

Polynesia centuries before Tasman's
arrival.

The Dutch would come to know the islands
as New Zealand.
So when was this place discovered?
The answer depends on who is asking.
And the same question changes the story of
how people discovered the world.
Our story begins much earlier,
in Africa, where our species,
Homo sapiens, emerged.

Over many generations, groups of people
moved beyond
Africa into other regions.
This was not a single expedition,
with a shared destination or a map.
Landscapes changed, coastlines shifted,
and people moved through a world we cannot
fully reconstruct. In the Middle East,

remains of our species are roughly ninety
thousand years old.
That is evidence people were there,
not a record of every step they took.

Farther east, people reached the great
landmass that

included present-day Australia and New
Guinea.

People were living in Australia at least
fifty
thousand years ago.
Sea levels were lower then,

joining Australia and New Guinea into one
landmass.
But even at lower sea levels,

open water separated it from Southeast
Asia.
Someone had to cross the sea,
long before the charts we know today.
We do not know the exact route,

the first landing, or the first arrival
date.

In Europe, too, evidence places Homo
sapiens there
more than forty-five thousand years ago.
Neanderthals, another kind of human,

were already living across parts of
Eurasia.

Across the planet, falling seas also
exposed land
between northeastern Asia and Alaska.
This broad region, called Beringia,

connected places that are separated by
water today.

But the precise routes and timing of
people's

journeys into the Americas remain
uncertain.
In what is now New Mexico,

human footprints survive beside an ancient
lake.

Those footprints date to roughly
twenty-three to twenty-one
thousand years ago.
The footprints do not tell us who arrived
first, or which way they came.

They tell us that people were already
living
there by that time.

Far south, people lived in present-day
Chile around
fourteen thousand five hundred years ago.

Over time, many different peoples
developed across the

Americas, with their own histories and
connections.

By now, people lived in many parts of the
world.
Was the world discovered?
Not in the same way for everyone.

Different communities knew different parts
of it.
A sailor knew coasts and currents;
a trader carried news from farther away.
Stories, journeys, and observations

gradually built larger pictures of the
world.

One surviving Babylonian map shows how its
makers
imagined the world around them.
It is a view from one place,
not a record of everything humanity knew.

Meanwhile, knowledge passed between people
across Africa,
Asia, and Europe through travel and trade.
Across the North Atlantic,

another journey reached a shore already
known to others.

Norse voyagers crossed from Greenland to
Newfoundland,
on the edge of North America.
At a settlement there,
wood was cut in the year ten twenty-one.
That date proves a Norse presence,
not the year the first Norse ship arrived.

Indigenous peoples had already lived in
the region
long before the Norse arrived.

Other maps were drawing together knowledge
from communities
around a different sea.

In twelfth-century Sicily, the mapmaker
al-Idrisi assembled accounts
of lands and routes.

His work drew on information from many
places,

including lands he had not necessarily
visited.
But maps on paper were only one way
to carry knowledge across great distances.
In the Pacific, navigators read the stars,
ocean swells, and signs from birds.

They carried knowledge of distant islands
and ocean
routes across generations.

From East Polynesia, settlers eventually
reached the islands
we call New Zealand.

Permanent settlement dates to the late
thirteenth century;
first arrival may have been earlier.

Those settlers became ancestors of Māori
communities,
long before Tasman's ships appeared.
On the other side of Asia,
ships were connecting already busy ports.

For centuries, trade linked communities
around the Indian
Ocean, from Asia to East Africa.
In the early fifteenth century,

Chinese fleets led by Zheng He sailed
through these waters.
Some voyages reached East Africa,

visiting ports that were already part of
those networks.

The world was connecting in many
directions,
not waiting for one group to open it.

Then an Atlantic voyage brought two worlds
into
a connection with immense consequences.

In fourteen ninety-two, Christopher
Columbus reached Caribbean islands
while sailing west from Europe.
He had not reached an empty world.

Taíno people already lived on those
islands.
The encounter began a period of conquest,
forced labor, and devastating disease.

These changes unfolded over time and
brought catastrophe
to Indigenous communities.

For Europeans, reports from the Atlantic
forced a
new question: what lay across the ocean?
In fifteen oh seven,

a world map printed the name America on
South America.

The map also showed land separated from
Asia
by an ocean to the west.

Its unusual outline was not yet an
accurate
picture of the whole Pacific.
But a voyage was about to make the
scale of that ocean impossible to ignore.

In fifteen nineteen, an expedition led by
Ferdinand
Magellan sailed west from Spain.
The ships passed the southern tip of South
America and entered the Pacific Ocean.

The crossing was far longer and more
punishing
than the crew had expected.
Magellan was killed in the Philippines,

before the expedition could complete its
journey.

In fifteen twenty-two, the ship Victoria
returned to
Spain under Juan Sebastián Elcano.
The expedition had circled the globe,

but Magellan himself had not completed the
voyage.

Educated people already knew Earth was
round;
the voyage revealed its vast,
connected oceans.
Yet a journey around the world did not
mean every coast was known to everyone.
That brings us back to the coast Tasman
approached in sixteen forty-two.

Māori communities had been living in New
Zealand
for generations before the Dutch arrived.
After a violent encounter,
in which four of his men were killed,
Tasman sailed away.
He left without landing.

For the Dutch, these islands were newly
encountered land.
For people already living there,
this was a new arrival,
not a discovery of home.

One great continent remained beyond these
stories of
settlement and contact: Antarctica.
In the seventeen seventies,

James Cook sailed around the southern seas
without
seeing the continent.

Ice and immense distances kept the land
itself out of sight.

In eighteen twenty, several expeditions
sighted parts of
the Antarctic coast.

Even then, its complete coastline and
interior were
still far from understood.
Today, a world map can look like a
single, finished answer.
But it brings together many stories:
migration, navigation, local knowledge,
trade, and mapping.

A place can have different dates for
settlement,
contact, and appearance on a map.
To understand any date of discovery,

ask one question: who discovered this
place, and for whom?
